title: The Poetry of Abhinavagupta
claim: Abhinavagupta’s nine hymns, printed whole and decoded verse by verse: not a selection of famous lines but the complete poetry, sharp enough to read in one sitting and exact enough to trust.

purpose.impact: One sitting with the whole of Abhinavagupta’s poetry, decoded verse by verse, until the philosopher disappears and only the voice remains.
purpose.reader: Readers who know the name and have never heard him sing; practitioners tired of commentary; anyone who wants the poems themselves.
purpose.realisation: The doctrine is not argued here — it is addressed. The reader catches themselves being addressed, and the address is the recognition.
non_goals: no critical apparatus or variant readings
no paraphrase in place of translation
no selection of greatest hits — the hymns are printed whole

pages.note: 172 verses at ~3/pp (58pp) + 9 hymn openers + front 10 + glossary 8 + index 6 + end 4 = 95, padded to 108. Study edition (400pp) is a later annotated printing, not a new volume.

sections_plan.purpose: the terrifying Lord praised — awe as the first door
the deity in the body — the body as mandala
the goddess of time — sequence, memory, the wheel
twelve verses on the highest truth
fifty verses at the end of the path
the examination of the highest truth — the poet’s own voice

inclusion: all verses of the source, in order, set continuously at two to three per page
each chapter opens with a short argument placed from ARGMAP + C1, never newly written
glossary terms and definitions are placed from C1 key terms; index is generated
all 172 verses of the nine hymns, in the hymns’ own order, decoded and translated
each hymn opens with a one-page orientation placed from C1; no other editorial prose
exclusion: no verse may be selected away to make room — the argument requires the whole set
no verse from this source may appear in another book
no facing-page commentary in the reference edition; that is the expanded edition's job
no verse is selected away and none is reserved for a later volume — this is the complete reference
no commentary between verses; the poem is the object
